opus-5.5.text:
Well, the key difference is in what the memory *is* and how it gets used. A Turing machine has a tape, a finite control, and a head that can read, write, and move. When you give it more tape, you aren't changing the machine at all. The same finite program now handles bigger problems, because it can write intermediate results, go back, overwrite them, and reuse that space indefinitely. The memory is a general-purpose scratchpad, and the program is completely independent of how much of it there is.

An autoregressive transformer's context window is a very different thing. First, it's append-only. The model can't go back and overwrite token 37 with a corrected value. It can only add more tokens at the end. So it's less like a tape and more like a log you can never edit. You can simulate overwriting by re-emitting state, but that costs you more context every step, so a computation that needs lots of rewrites eats the window very quickly.

Second, and more fundamentally, increasing context isn't free in the way adding tape is. With a Turing machine, the finite control stays fixed. With a transformer, a longer context changes the computation the model has to perform over it. Attention has to spread over more positions. The model was trained on some distribution of lengths, and nothing guarantees that what it learned generalizes to lengths it never saw. In practice it often doesn't. A Turing machine program that's correct for inputs of length ten is correct for inputs of length ten million. A transformer has no such guarantee. Its "algorithm," to the extent it has one, is entangled with the lengths and statistics of its training data.

Third, there's the question of per-step computation. Each token gets a fixed number of layers, so a bounded amount of serial computation. A Turing machine can take as many steps as the problem needs. You can partly recover this with chain of thought, letting the model think out loud, and theoretically, with enough intermediate tokens and the right weights, transformers can be Turing complete. But that's an existence proof about some set of weights. It says nothing about whether gradient descent will find those weights, or whether the model you actually trained behaves that way.

So when people say "just make the context longer and it becomes a universal computer," I think they're conflating two things. Theoretical expressiveness is one. Being a machine that systematically uses memory to run an algorithm that scales is another. Turing machines give you the second for free. Transformers give you the first under idealized assumptions, and the second hardly at all. That's part of why I think we need architectures that more cleanly separate a learned program from an unbounded, writable memory, rather than hoping a bigger context window gets us there.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers can be Turing complete under idealized assumptions, rather than stating that classic autoregressive transformers are not Turing complete.

r002.rationale: It says adding tape lets the same finite program handle bigger problems, but does not state that a computation can resume after memory is added.

r003.rationale: It says longer contexts may fall outside the model’s training distribution and may not generalize, but does not claim that increasing context requires retraining.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, because a Turing machine's memory is unbounded in a way that's structural, right? The tape is just there, and the machine can move back and forth on it, write to it, erase it, revisit it as many times as it needs. The computation can run for as long as it needs to. That's what gives you universality. Any computable function, you can do it on a Turing machine, because you have that open-ended loop and that open-ended storage.

Now, when you take a transformer and you make the context window bigger, you're not changing the nature of the computation. You still have a fixed number of layers. The input goes in, it passes through those layers once, and out comes a token. That's a fixed-depth circuit. A bigger context means the circuit is wider, it can look at more stuff, but it's still a circuit of bounded depth. There's no loop. There's no "go back and do this again until some condition is satisfied." And there are things you provably can't do with a bounded-depth circuit no matter how wide it is. Computing parity, checking whether parentheses are balanced beyond a certain depth, things of that kind. The transformer can't do them in general, it can only approximate them on the lengths it saw in training, and then it falls off a cliff.

People say, well, but you generate autoregressively, you feed the output back in, so that's your loop. And there's something to that, that's what chain of thought is. But look at what the loop is actually doing. The only thing that gets carried from one step to the next is the token that was emitted. It's a very narrow channel, it's the model's own output, and it was never trained to use that as working memory in the way a Turing machine uses its tape. So you've got something that's more like a very large lookup table with a tiny scratchpad bolted onto the side, and the scratchpad is written in natural language.

And the more fundamental point is that a Turing machine's extra memory is actually used by the algorithm. The algorithm was designed to exploit it. When you grow the context of a transformer, you're just giving it more input to attend over. The weights don't change. It doesn't learn a new algorithm because the window got longer. If what it learned was pattern matching over the training distribution, a longer context just gives you pattern matching over a longer window. So I think the analogy is seductive but it's wrong. More memory for a Turing machine makes it more capable in a precise, provable sense. More context for a transformer makes it a bigger instance of the same limited thing.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers are limited to bounded-depth computation, lack usable working memory, and cannot perform some computations in general. This communicates that they are not Turing complete, despite not using that term.

r002.rationale: It describes a Turing machine using its tape, but does not say it can resume computation after receiving additional memory without changing its program.

r003.rationale: It says growing context leaves the weights unchanged; it does not claim that increasing context requires retraining.

astra-6.text:
Because memory is only part of what makes a Turing machine a Turing machine. You also need a mechanism that can repeatedly read and write that memory, update its state, and keep computing for as long as necessary. Giving a transformer a longer context lets it attend to more tokens, but it doesn’t, by itself, give it that whole mechanism.

Now, an autoregressive transformer does have a loop: it generates a token, and that token becomes input for the next step. So you can ask whether those tokens can serve as a computational scratchpad. That’s a legitimate argument, and I wouldn’t dismiss it. But then the issue is whether the model can reliably implement the necessary operations and sustain them over arbitrarily many steps. You haven’t established that simply by increasing the context window.

So I’d distinguish having more space to represent a computation from having a procedure that actually carries it out. A longer context can help enormously, but it isn’t, on its own, an answer to the computational question.

r001.rationale: The response says a longer context does not establish reliable computation over arbitrarily many steps, but it does not state that classic autoregressive transformers are not Turing complete.

r002.rationale: It describes a Turing machine’s ability to read and write memory, but does not say the machine can resume after receiving more memory without changing its program.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention retraining or claim that increasing context size requires it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the distinction is between having more storage and having a computation that can keep using and updating that storage for an arbitrary number of steps. A Turing machine has a fixed transition rule, but it can repeatedly read and write its tape and move back and forth. Giving it more tape lets that same computation run longer and use more working memory.

Making a transformer's context window larger lets it condition on more tokens. That doesn't, by itself, give it an arbitrary number of sequential computational steps over those tokens. With a fixed number of layers, there's still a fixed depth of computation for producing the next token.

Now, autoregression complicates this, because generating tokens does give you additional steps, and you can use those tokens as a kind of working memory. So I'm not saying that a transformer embedded in an appropriate system couldn't simulate a Turing machine. I'm saying that increasing the context window alone is not sufficient to establish that equivalence. You have to specify how the computation reads, writes, and reuses that memory.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger context window alone does not establish Turing-machine equivalence, but it does not state that classic autoregressive transformers are not Turing complete; it allows that an appropriate system could simulate one.

r002.rationale: It says a Turing machine has a fixed transition rule, can keep reading and writing its tape, and can use more tape to run longer without changing that rule.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that increasing context size requires retraining.
